projects.title: L.A.R.A.
projects.subtitle: Lab Assistant Robot Arm
projects.summary: A six-axis workshop robot arm investigating motion-error compensation, with a modular tool changer in development.
projects.introduction:
L.A.R.A. (Lab Assistant Robot Arm) explores how a six-axis arm could become a flexible workshop assistant. The project brings together mechanical design, joint control, and research into tracking a desired motion more closely.

The research plan is to collect extensive motion data from the physical arm and use stochastic analysis to model the small, random errors seen during movement. The aim is to investigate whether adjusting motor targets can bring the actual position-versus-time trajectory closer to the intended one.

model.alt: Orthographic CAD model of the L.A.R.A. robot arm assembly

notes: The v1 arm is assembled; all joints have been tested separately.
The v2 arm design and 3D-printed parts are complete.
Stochastic analysis and target-position compensation are planned research.

projects.cardSummary: A six-axis workshop robot arm investigating motion-error compensation, with a modular tool changer in development.
projects.currentState:
**V1: assembled and tested joint by joint.** Each joint works separately on the real arm. Coordinated sequence and task testing are planned.

**V2: designed and printed.** The 3D design is complete and its parts have been 3D-printed. The first tool-changer design is also complete; issues found in that design are being addressed in its second version.

engineeringTopics.title: From individual joints to coordinated motion
engineeringTopics.body: The v1 assembly has been checked one joint at a time. Coordinated trajectories and workshop tasks remain to be tested.

engineeringTopics.title: Learn from motion error
engineeringTopics.body: The planned study will record real joint motion, compare actual and target position over time, and use stochastic analysis to investigate error patterns. Predicting and compensating future tracking error is the research objective.

engineeringTopics.title: Interchangeable tools
engineeringTopics.body: A first tool-changer design has been completed. Its identified issues are being revised for v2 before tool swapping can be evaluated as part of a working task.

nextSteps: Collect position-versus-time data from the physical arm and compare it with the target trajectory.
Investigate whether stochastic models of the tracking error can improve motor-target compensation.
Evaluate coordinated motion and the revised tool changer before attempting workshop tasks.

projects.title: Pop-up Spoiler
projects.subtitle: Two ESP32 boards translate adjustable roll and pitch response curves into coordinated motion for four encoder-feedback motors.
projects.summary: A two-wing spoiler prototype with coordinated motor control and adjustable responses to sensed roll and pitch.
projects.introduction:
This project explores active aerodynamics through a pop-up spoiler prototype for a third-generation BMW 6 Series. The design allows each wing panel to move independently.

The goal is to coordinate the motors and linkages so the wings follow adjustable responses to sensed roll and pitch. A tunable controller makes it possible to compare different responses and test the mechanism before evaluating its behavior under driving and aerodynamic loads.

media.alt: Orthographic CAD model of the pop-up spoiler and its two actuator linkages

model.alt: Orthographic CAD model of the pop-up spoiler and its two actuator linkages

notes: Four bars, one guided motion: each wing rides on connected arms that lift and tilt it along a defined path.

Getting the dimensions right: arm lengths and pivot spacing must produce the required lift, tilt, and clearance together. Near the flat starting position, small errors or joint play can make the linkage bind or move unpredictably.
Two motors per wing: powering both arms is intended to share the load. The unequal arms need different, coordinated angles; encoder feedback helps each motor follow its coordinated target.

Tune the response visually: set the sensor's neutral reference, then drag curve points or enter values to choose how sensed roll and pitch move the wings. Three presets let different responses be compared.

Wing angles first, motor angles second: roll gives a mirrored left/right response, while pitch acts on both wings. The curves combine into 0–70° wing commands, and the linkage calculation converts each command into two motor targets.

Keep motion separate from the dashboard: one ESP32 handles sensing and tuning; the other controls the motors. Manual wing and individual-motor modes help check the mechanism before trying automatic operation.

Test the physical result: position feedback corrects tracking errors, and lost encoder data or communication disarms the motors. The sensor estimates tilt from acceleration, so response under braking, cornering, and aerodynamic load still needs testing.

specs.label: Actuation
specs.value: 4 DC motors with magnetic position feedback

bom.detail: Two ESP32 DevKit boards: N1 for motor control, N2 for sensing and the dashboard
MPU6050 accelerometer and gyroscope module; current wing commands use accelerometer-derived roll and pitch
Four MT6701 magnetic encoders, one per motor
125 mm and 100 mm arms, 55 mm motor-shaft spacing, and a 30 mm wing-carrying connecting link per side

projects.cardSummary: A two-wing spoiler prototype with coordinated motor control and adjustable responses to sensed roll and pitch.
projects.currentState:
The project combines a mechanical prototype with two ESP32 firmwares for sensing, tuning, and coordinated motor control. Its controller supports manual checks and automatic responses to sensed roll and pitch.

Behavior under braking, cornering, and aerodynamic loads still needs physical testing. The present controller estimates tilt from acceleration.

engineeringTopics.title: Two wings, four motors
engineeringTopics.body: Each wing rides on a four-bar linkage. Two motors per wing follow coordinated, unequal angles to lift and tilt the panel along its intended path. Encoder feedback helps the motors track their targets.

engineeringTopics.title: Wing commands become motor targets
engineeringTopics.body: Roll gives a mirrored left/right response, while pitch acts on both wings. Adjustable curves combine into 0–70° wing commands; a linkage calculation converts each command into two motor targets.

engineeringTopics.title: Tune before automatic operation
engineeringTopics.body: Set the sensor’s neutral reference, then drag curve points or enter values in the local dashboard. Three presets, manual wing control, and individual-motor modes support checking and comparing responses.

engineeringTopics.title: Separate control and supervision
engineeringTopics.body: One ESP32 handles sensing and tuning; the other controls the motors. The firmware disarms the motors when encoder data or communication is lost. Physical travel, clearance, and tracking still need to be checked on the assembled mechanism.

nextSteps: Check assembled linkage clearance and synchronized tracking across the commanded range.
Evaluate the sensing and control response under realistic motion and aerodynamic loads.

projects.title: Tekkai 2.0
projects.subtitle: An autonomous sumo robot with three ultrasonic sensors, two edge sensors, remote motor enable, and an onboard Wi-Fi debug interface.
projects.summary: An autonomous sumo robot with ultrasonic opponent tracking, front edge sensing, remote motor enable, and an onboard Wi-Fi debug interface.
projects.introduction:
Tekkai 2.0 was built to find an opponent, push it out of a sumo ring, and avoid crossing the boundary without a driver. The project brings mechanical design, opponent sensing, and autonomous control together under a tight budget.

The 2026 version builds on the 2024 robot with four-wheel drive, infrared edge detection, stronger motors, and revised ultrasonic sensing logic.

media.alt: Orthographic CAD model of the Tekkai 2.0 sumo robot assembly

model.alt: Orthographic CAD model of the Tekkai 2.0 sumo robot assembly

notes: Three ultrasonic channels classify the opponent direction using a 40 cm detection threshold. Valid target readings take priority over edge detection; the controller searches toward the last detected side when no target is visible.

The two active-low edge inputs require two consecutive confirmations. Without an ultrasonic target, both edges trigger a 500 ms reverse followed by a left search; individual edges cause an evasive turn.

The robot boots OFF. Remote ON/OFF inputs control the motor-driver enable output, and the local Wi-Fi page provides manual ON/OFF, a motor test, sensor readings, and motor PWM telemetry. The separately linked 2024 firmware is historical.

projects.cardSummary: An autonomous sumo robot with ultrasonic opponent tracking, front edge sensing, remote motor enable, and an onboard Wi-Fi debug interface.
projects.currentState:
The current 2026 firmware combines three ultrasonic opponent sensors, two front edge sensors, remote ON/OFF inputs, a motor-driver enable output, and a local Wi-Fi debug interface. It boots with the motors disabled.

Opponent pursuit takes priority: when an ultrasonic target is detected, the controller drives toward it. Edge detection is evaluated only while the ultrasonic sensors are clear.

projects.title: CupExS Drag Racer
projects.subtitle: An educational physics experiment kit designed for Cup of Experimental Science 2026.
projects.summary: A hands-on physics kit for investigating how gear ratio changes a small car’s acceleration, speed, and stopping behavior.
projects.introduction:
Built for the Cup of Experimental Science 2026, this drag racer turns a drivetrain design decision into a hands-on physics experiment: which gear ratio produces the quickest 10-metre run?

The goal is to compare how gearing balances wheel torque and speed, then test those predictions with measured runs. A companion motor dyno and two-lane timing system provide tools for investigating motor behavior and comparing results.

media.alt: Orthographic CAD model of the CupExS drag racer with yellow bodywork and blue wheels

model.alt: Orthographic CAD model of the CupExS drag racer with yellow bodywork and blue wheels

notes: The current car controller provides browser Start / Stop commands, 20 kHz 10-bit forward PWM, and an automatic stop after a 60-second run window.

A separate ESP32 timer alternates 36 kHz bursts across two lanes, handles a countdown, and records independent finish times when beams are interrupted. Vehicle launch and lane timing use separate controllers.
The companion dyno firmware samples an MT6701 encoder and ACS712 current sensor and estimates torque and power from a configured inertia.

Vehicle launch and lane timing are controlled independently.

projects.title: Door Security System
projects.subtitle: An ESP32 door monitor combines an infrared beam, motion-based tamper detection, a buzzer, a local web panel, and optional email alerts.
projects.summary: A lab door monitor that detects beam interruptions and movement, sounds an alarm, and can send email alerts.
projects.introduction:
Built to help protect the lab, this project combines a door-monitoring infrared beam with motion-based tamper detection. It brings the sensors, alarm, and controls into a system that can be checked from a local web panel.

The goal is to flag a confirmed beam interruption or disturbance while armed, sound a local alarm, and optionally send an email alert. Confirmation delays help distinguish sustained events from brief sensor disturbances.
notes: The controller emits NEC-coded IR at 38 kHz and watches receiver CH1. A confirmed beam interruption while armed latches the alarm.
MPU6050 tilt, angular speed, and acceleration changes are checked against a calibrated baseline, with a confirmation interval to reject brief disturbances.
The web panel switches Open / Armed modes and shows a bounded breach log. Wi-Fi credentials and Gmail app credentials are supplied locally.

projects.cardSummary: A lab door monitor that detects beam interruptions and movement, sounds an alarm, and can send email alerts.
projects.currentState: The controller implements infrared beam monitoring, motion-based tamper detection, a local alarm, and a web panel. Email alerts are optional and depend on local configuration. Confirmation intervals reject brief disturbances before an alarm is latched.

projects.title: GYM Scale
projects.subtitle: A BLE-connected ESP32 load-cell scale with filtered weight telemetry and a Flutter companion app for local measurements and food logging.
projects.summary: A Bluetooth-connected weighing platform with a companion app for recording measurements and food logs locally.
projects.introduction:
A weight reading becomes more useful when it can be recorded alongside what was measured. GYM Scale connects a physical weighing platform to a companion app, bringing weight measurements and food logging into one workflow.

The goal is to produce stable readings, send them wirelessly over Bluetooth Low Energy, and keep food and measurement records locally in the app. The project brings together load-cell electronics, signal filtering, and a mobile interface.

media.alt: GYM Scale CAD model with a blue weighing platform and front controls
media.caption: GYM Scale enclosure and weighing-platform design.

notes: HX711 readings pass through a median window and a Kalman-style denoiser after startup tare. The configured calibration factor and 10 kg capacity must match the actual load cell.
A versioned 16-byte BLE packet carries readiness flags, sequence, uptime, grams, and raw delta. Notifications are limited to a 200 ms interval.
The Flutter app scans and subscribes over BLE, checks packet validity and stale readings, and uses local SQLite storage for food and measurement workflows. This is a prototype platform.

gallery.alt: GYM Scale browser interface showing a weight readout, tare and mode controls, and food nutrition information
gallery.caption: Browser interface with weight, tare controls, and food nutrition information.

projects.cardSummary: A Bluetooth-connected weighing platform with a companion app for recording measurements and food logs locally.
projects.currentState: The prototype combines load-cell firmware with a Flutter app for BLE measurements and local food and measurement records. Its software filters the sensor readings and marks stale or invalid packets. The configured capacity and calibration must match the physical load cell.
